endorsements.quote: Implementation typically requires the clear specification of permitted actions, definite stop points preventing unauthorized actions regardless of the agent’s recommendations, and clear escalation pathways when agents encounter situations outside their defined scope.

Boundaries must be specified across multiple dimensions: clinical scope (eg, which situations and which patient populations), authority to act (eg, information retrieval and order entry), and decision risk (eg, routine monitoring and critical interventions).

Agents function as assistive tools supporting the clinical decision-making process; ultimate responsibility for patient care rests with licensed professionals who have the authority to accept, modify, or reject agent recommendations.
Complete auditability requires recording not only agent outputs but also the reasoning processes, data sources, and intermediate steps that led to those outputs [ 30 ].
Confidence scores and uncertainty estimates should trigger mandatory human review when agents encounter unusual situations.
Postdeployment monitoring collects performance data across patient encounters and identifies systematic errors, shifts in behavior over time, or performance differences among patient subgroups.

Recovery and decay models assess how agents respond to errors, ambiguous inputs, or missing data, determining whether they fail by escalating appropriately or produce unreliable outputs without signaling the ambiguity.

unlisted_practices: Validate medical AI agents before deployment across anticipated clinical scenarios, including edge cases and ambiguous presentations, using domain experts to evaluate intermediate reasoning steps and tool calls.
Evaluate agentic AI on end-to-end task reliability and constraint compliance rather than predictive accuracy alone.
Expand agent autonomy boundaries gradually only after reliable performance is demonstrated through formal validation processes.
Log reflective outputs of agents and link them to predefined update policies rather than allowing continuous unsupervised adaptation.
Document which actions were initiated by agents, which were approved by clinicians, and the justification for deviations from agent recommendations.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary discussing the governance, architectural safeguards (bounded autonomy, verification, auditability), and deployment considerations of medical AI agents using the PARM framework.
